text:

The Council doubles down on the Commission’s deregulatory agenda
When the European Commission presented its Digital Omnibus in November 2025, it promised to simplify Europe’s digital rules without weakening fundamental rights. Yet, as EDRi and others warned at the time, a majority of its proposals, particularly those regarding General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and ePrivacy, went far beyond reducing administrative burdens. They are part and parcel of a broad deregulatory wave that is devouring most of our rights and safeguards in the name of empty promises of competitiveness and sovereignty.
On 21 October 2026, EU governments agreed on their negotiating position, which has timidly corrected some of the Commission’s most questionable choices, but has mainly endorsed changes that could make exploiting personal data easier while making abuses even harder to challenge.
The result is a deal that weakens important safeguards and makes redress harder. There is also little evidence that weakening these protections will improve Europe’s competitiveness. Some changes may instead reinforce the advantages of Big Tech companies that already control and abuse enormous volumes of information about us and the people around us.
AI companies get a helping hand to use even more personal data
One of the most worrying changes concerns the use of personal data for AI.
The Council retained a dedicated provision, Article 88bis (Article 88c in the Commission’s proposal), explicitly recognising the possibility of relying on the GDPR’s ‘legitimate interest’ legal basis to use personal data when developing or operating AI systems. Under the GDPR, companies can already use this legal basis in certain circumstances, provided they demonstrate a legitimate interest, prove that processing is necessary, and establish that people’s rights do not override that interest.
The Council clarifies that AI development does not automatically constitute a legitimate interest and that existing conditions still apply. But if legitimate interests can already justify certain AI processing, why introduce a special provision?
The concern is that Article 88bis could tilt the legitimate interest assessment in favour of AI companies, giving preferential treatment to a vaguely defined set of technologies primarily owned by autocracy-supporting billionaires, regardless of the exact purpose for which our personal data is going to be used. As recent legal analysis explains, this risks changing how the existing balancing test between legitimate interest and data protection safeguards is applied, even without formally removing its requirements.
Companies could invoke this legislative endorsement to justify extensive data reuse, even when people never reasonably expected their information to be used for AI training. And who benefits most? The same dominant Big Tech corporations that have spent decades accumulating the most intimate information about billions of people.
The Council also retains an exception for sensitive personal data appearing incidentally in AI datasets (proposed Article 9(2)(k) and 9(2)), including information revealing health, political opinions or religious beliefs. Companies must try to avoid collecting and, where collected, remove such data, but may retain them under safeguards when removal proves technically impossible or requires manifestly disproportionate effort.
These conditions might look important, but risk turning difficulties in cleaning datasets into a justification for retaining highly sensitive information. In opaque AI systems, verifying whether such data have genuinely been isolated may often be impossible. In this regard we should bear in mind that companies are mandated to protect our data and rights, and technical choices should not determine how far our fundamental rights extend.

title: Independent study on the impact of age assurance on fundamental rights and costs for businesses
text:
Age assurance is key for a safer online environment as it ensures that children only access online services and features that are safe and age appropriate for them. Nowadays, 1 in 3 children, aged 9 to 11 across 6 European countries, reports having a social media profile. Very few services are implementing age assurance in a systematic way.
To further strengthen the preparation of the proposed EU KIDS Act and the accompanying Staff Working Document, the European Commission procured a study to:

Analyse the impact of age assurance on key fundamental rights, including data protection and privacy, non-discrimination, freedom of expression and access to information;
Assess the potential financial impacts of age assurance on businesses, including micro and small enterprises.

The study was carried out by an external contractor. It does not assess the proposed EU KIDS Act and the compliance by any specific service provider.
The study's key insights are:

Fundamental rights – an age assurance framework can be both proportionate and respectful of fundamental rights. Interferences with those rights can be mitigated through appropriate safeguards. In particular, the framework should ensure:

Data protection and privacy – legislative coherence with the GDPR, high standards of privacy and security, and the development of technical standards;
Non-discrimination, freedom of expression and access to information – minimising friction for users, ensuring transparency, promoting user empowerment where appropriate through greater choice, and ensuring inclusivity and accessibility.

EU approach to age verification – the EU age verification blueprint can make an important contribution to the development of a coherent EU-level approach to age assurance. Specifically, the findings suggest that:

the blueprint has the potential to become one of the most affordable ways for service providers of all sizes to comply with age assurance requirements because it is privacy-preserving and open by design and its development costs have been publicly subsidised;
the roll-out of the blueprint across all Member States should be accelerated;
the provision and resourcing of effective fallback enrollment routes – including manual enrolment options at national and local level – should be ensured.

Costs for businesses – online services would inevitably face new costs. However, these costs are likely to remain modest for most services and to decrease over time, due to:

competition in the third-party vendor market,
the emergence of technical standards,
improvements in interoperability,
the availability of the EU age verification blueprint.

For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), the study suggests that it's unlikely to face excessive costs, thanks to affordable, ready-to-use age verification solutions and competition between providers. They will also benefit from having a common set of EU rules, rather than having to comply with different national requirements.

title: Call for evidence on advertising repositories
text:
Opening: 04 November 2026

Closing: 02 December 2026

The feedback is being gathered through a call for evidence.
The responses collected through the call for evidence will help shape guidelines aimed at ensuring that advertising repositories meet the needs of their users. Amongst other things, the guidelines will advise on:

how to make advertising repositories easily searchable
how to provide insights on how users are targeted and reached
how to make the content of advertisements accessible

Once adopted, these guidelines will aim to ensure that the advertising repositories provided by very large online platforms (VLOPs) and very large online search engines (VLOSEs) are effective and fit for purpose.
Effective advertising repositories are essential tools for enabling greater public scrutiny of online advertising. Transparency in advertising – revealing who pays and how citizens are targeted – helps to protect public health, ensure a high level of consumer protection and safeguard the integrity of elections. Advertising repositories also support effective supervision and enforcement of the DSA.
Next steps
The call for evidence will be followed by a targeted public consultation in 2027. Researchers, civil society, providers of VLOPs and VLOSEs and representatives from the advertising industry will be invited to share feedback on a draft version of the guidelines. The publication of the guidelines is planned for the second quarter of 2028.
Background
Under Article 39 of the DSA, providers of VLOPs and VLOSEs are required to maintain publicly accessible repositories of advertisements displayed on their services. These repositories (commonly known as ‘ad libraries’) provide information on the content of advertisements, who paid for them, the period during which they were displayed, how many users the advertisements reached, and the main criteria used to decide who saw the advertisements.
Article 39(3) of the DSA provides the possibility for the Commission to issue guidelines on the design of advertising repositories, following consultation with the European Board for Digital Services, researchers and the public. The guidelines will support the Commission’s supervision and enforcement of VLOPs and VLOSEs’ compliance with Article 39 of the DSA.

GPUStack is an open-source GPU cluster manager for AI model serving and GPU instance provisioning. The Russia-linked threat actor known as APT29 is said to be behind a large-scale watering hole campaign targeting iOS and Android users through compromised websites, fake domains, and a supply chain attack involving a Ukrainian web analytics service called Plerdy SEO Tracker.

"The injected JavaScript code collects browser and device attributes," Sekoia researchers Amaury-Jacques Garçon and Félix Aime said in a technical report shared with The Hacker News. "Then, the delivery infrastructure delivers a platform-specific N-day exploit chain targeting either iOS or Android."

The end goal of the attacks is to serve payloads capable of stealing browser cookies, and in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords or full mobile device data. The activity, codenamed Poisoned Source, was discovered by the French cybersecurity company in mid-October 2026.

A defining aspect of the campaign is the use of three infection vectors -

Compromise of legitimate websites to inject malicious JavaScript
Lookalike sites masquerading as high-profile websites in the U.S. ("america250[.]holiday"), Ukraine, Czech Republic, and Bulgaria
Supply chain compromise of Plerdy SEO Tracker between August 27 and September 3, 2026, by injecting malicious code into "a.plerdy[.]com/public/js/click/main.js"

Some of the compromised websites include a major industry trade association representing U.S. companies operating in the chemical industry, a far-right European political party, and a Bulgarian military-related website. It's suspected that the watering hole campaign may have been designed to target specific individuals rather than a broad effort.

"It remains unclear whether the attackers intended to target visitors to specific websites or sought to compromise as many unpatched mobile devices as possible, indiscriminately exfiltrating data before selectively identifying and exploiting information of interest," Sekoia said.

"However, several of these sites are likely to attract high-value or strategically important visitors in the context of the Russia-Ukraine war. This supply chain attack spread through high-value targets, such as army, special forces, and military equipment (ballistic, UAV) websites."

Regardless of the method employed, all roads lead to the same payload: a JavaScript loader that profiles the visitor's device and web browser, and then serves appropriate next-stage malware. For iOS users, it leads to an exploit kit called DarkSword to harvest cookies and full device data.

On Android, the malware is equipped to exfiltrate Chrome data and Wi-Fi passwords without establishing persistence. No less than three different exploits have been identified -

Class A, which targets iOS devices running iOS 16.7 and exploits CVE-2025-43529 (the same vulnerability exploited by DarkSword) and CVE-2024-27834 to deliver JavaScript malware for cookie theft.

title: Critical Rails Flaw Lets Attackers Write Server Files via Crafted ImageMagick Uploads
text:
Critical Rails Flaw Lets Attackers Write Server Files via Crafted ImageMagick UploadsSwati KhandelwalNov 04, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security

//<![CDATA[

//]]>

A critical flaw in Ruby on Rails could allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on an app's server by uploading a crafted file if the app processes uploads using ImageMagick. The Rails project disclosed the flaw in an advisory and fixed it in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

The flaw is in Active Storage, the part of Rails that handles file uploads. Some apps store uploaded files using Active Storage's Disk service, which stores them on the server's disk. In those apps, an attacker could also read any file the app can read.

Those files typically include the app's secret_key_base and its credentials for other systems, according to Rails. Reading them may in turn allow remote code execution or lateral movement into those systems.

Rails rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. It is tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 and does not yet have a CVE identifier.

ImageMagick selects a format handler, which it calls a coder, based on the file's content. Some coders act on other files named inside the image, not on the image itself. Active Storage imposes no limits on which coders an upload can use, so the server's own ImageMagick policy was the only limit.

The ImageMagick analyzer in Active Storage runs when a file is attached. Attaching the upload is enough to reach the flaw. The app does not have to make a variant (a transformed copy of the image) or a preview, or call analyze.

An uploaded SVG file reached ImageMagick's MSL coder through that analyzer, according to the commit that fixed the flaw. MSL is a scripting coder that reads and writes files named by its script.

Rails said one attack chain was reported to it, but it does "not assume it is the only one that exists." The advisory does not say whether the flaw has been exploited.

The flaw was reported through HackerOne by RyotaK, a researcher at GMO Flatt Security.

Which Rails Apps Are Affected

An app is affected only if all three of these are true:

It uses ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing. That is the setting config.active_storage.variant_processor = :mini_magick, the default for apps on load_defaults 6.1 or earlier.
Its ImageMagick security policy does not already block the coders involved. Rails says the policies that Debian and Ubuntu ship do not.
It accepts file uploads from untrusted users.

To check the first condition, look at config.active_storage.variant_processor. If it is not set, the default depends on load_defaults: :mini_magick before 7.0, and :vips from 7.0 on. The same setting decides which library analyzes uploads, not only which one makes variants.

Every Active Storage version before 8.0.5.2 is affected, as are 8.1 versions before 8.1.4.1. Release series older than 8.0 are no longer supported, and Rails will not release fixed versions for them.

In July, Rails fixed a different critical Active Storage flaw, CVE-2026-66066, which affected apps that use libvips instead of ImageMagick. Apps using ImageMagick were not exposed to that flaw's attack path, but they can be exposed to this one.

The same releases fix a second Active Storage flaw, GHSA-v924-7rp8-4mxh, which Rails rates high with a CVSS score of 8.8. Active Storage passed uploads to ImageMagick and FFmpeg under temporary file names that kept the uploaded file's extension.

Those tools can pick a decoder from the extension when a file's content does not show its format. So an attacker who chose an upload's filename and declared its content type could choose the decoder that processes it.

What to Do

Rails strongly recommends upgrading as soon as possible. The two releases fix 21 security issues in total.

text:
Xen Hypervisor Flaws Let One Malicious VM Read and Write Any Other VM's MemorySwati KhandelwalNov 04, 2026Vulnerability / Cloud Security

//<![CDATA[

//]]>

Two flaws in the Xen hypervisor allow a malicious guest virtual machine (VM) to read and write the memory of other VMs on the same host, including dom0.

Dom0 is the VM that, by default, has full permissions and manages the others. Patches are out, and there is no known mitigation, the Xen Project said in an advisory on November 3.

All Xen versions from 4.6 onward are vulnerable, while 4.5 and earlier are not. The flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-102703 and CVE-2026-102704, under Xen advisory XSA-523.

The Xen Project credited AI company Anthropic with finding the flaws using its Claude model. Stephan Lipp of Ada Logics then validated the finding, and the CodeAnt AI Security Research Team later independently reported the same issue.

The flaws are in grant copy, the operation Xen uses to copy data between VMs. Each VM tells Xen which of its memory pages other VMs may use, and Xen checks those permissions.

To save time on a batch of copies within the same memory page, Xen reuses checks it has already made. In some cases, it did not check again when it should have. That mistake is what lets a malicious guest read and write memory it does not own.

XCP-ng, an open-source virtualization platform built around Xen, said in its update notes that "a single compromised guest can break out of its isolation and take over the whole host."

Xen's advisory does not mention any attacks that exploit the flaws or specify what access within the VM an attacker needs.

Qubes OS is a security-focused desktop operating system that keeps software in separate Xen-based compartments called qubes. A bulletin said that every supported release and configuration is affected. Its fix is for Qubes 4.3, the only release it still supports.

Because every Xen version from 4.6 on is vulnerable, other products built on those versions are affected until their makers add the XSA-523 patches. As of November 4, Debian's security tracker listed the xen package in its bookworm, trixie, and forky releases as vulnerable, and in sid as fixed.

Fixes and Restarts by Platform

These are the fixes published so far:

Xen source: the advisory has patches for xen-unstable to Xen 4.19.x, and for Xen 4.18.x to 4.17.x.
Xen 4.6 to 4.16: the advisory has no patch for these versions. Xen 4.16's security support ended on December 2, 2024.
XCP-ng 8.3: xen-4.17.7-4.2.xcpng8.3, released November 3. Hosts must be rebooted. Vates, which backs XCP-ng, rates the impact as Critical.
Qubes OS 4.3: Xen packages 4.19.6-3 in dom0. Dom0 must be restarted, and Anti Evil Maid users must reseal their secret passphrase because the new Xen binaries change PCR18 and PCR19.

Qubes told users on November 3 to keep installing updates as normal. The fixed packages were then in its security-testing repository, due to move to the stable one over the next two weeks after community testing.

XSA-523 is separate from XSA-500, an earlier grant copy flaw that Xen disclosed on July 28, and it has its own patches.

A China-aligned threat actor known as SlippyNunchucks has been attributed to a Domain Name System (DNS) hijacking operation abusing insecure HTTP communications in Windows versions of Sogou Input Method as part of a surveillance campaign designed to deploy an implant called DarkVigil (aka FDMTP).

The campaign, observed starting July 1, 2026, is assessed to have targeted organizations and Chinese-speaking individuals in Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Oman, and Sri Lanka, according to ESET.

"DarkVigil implants are typically deployed through popular Chinese applications," ESET researcher Anh Ho said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "By abusing these applications, the SlippyNunchucks threat actor has been able to reach Chinese-speaking users across Asia and Europe."

Some of the applications abused by the adversary include Sogou Input Method, QuickFox, QingTalk, MiYunChat, SoftCam, and tawk.to.

Active since at least September 15, 2023, SlippyNunchucks is known for targeting organizations and Chinese-speaking individuals across South and East Asia. These attacks lead to the deployment of a modular .NET framework that includes DarkVigil and a set of over 20 plugins.

Although the use of the backdoor has been previously linked to Mustang Panda, ESET said it found no tactical overlaps between the threat actor and DarkVigil-related activity in its telemetry, prompting it to classify it as a distinct intrusion set.

Earlier this August, Fortinet's FortiGuard Incident Response Team detailed the threat actor's supply chain compromise of the QuickFox VPN and network acceleration tool to deliver DarkVigil.

According to the Slovakian cybersecurity company, the adversary shifted to exploiting Sogou Input Method, a popular Chinese-language input method editor developed by Tencent, as a delivery vector three days after QuickFox released a clean version of its program.

Specifically, the attack involves hijacking the app's branded vocabulary promotion mechanism to serve a malicious configuration, which ultimately paves the way for the deployment of the malware via SGTool.exe, a legitimate Sogou Input Method component that functions as a multi-purpose task dispatcher.

In a clean environment, the executable sends an HTTP request to the "config.pinyin.sogou[.]com/api/brandScd/getBrandScd.php" endpoint to fetch a configuration. But in the attack discovered by ESET, the DNS resolution of the domain is tampered with to resolve it to one of the two staging servers -

47.239.250[.]102 (sogou-cdn[.]com)
47.237.122[.]175 (dev.soft-png-cdn.com)

The consequence of this DNS hijacking was that HTTP requests to the "getBrandScd.php" endpoint were routed to one of the staging servers, which then responded with a malicious configuration. The configuration, for its part, instructs the binary to download two additional payloads from "sogou-cdn[.]com" and launch the malware via DLL sideloading -

A legitimate Adobe executable ("biz_helper.exe")
A rogue DLL ("libcef.dll") containing DarkVigil

DarkVigil is notable for its use of Duplex Message Transport Protocol (DMTP) for command-and-control (C2), allowing the client to execute and orchestrate plugins received from an attacker-controlled server to facilitate persistence or data collection.

Following responsible disclosure, Tencent addressed the vulnerability (CVE-2026-120422) in version 16.10, released on October 29, 2026, by migrating the affected HTTP requests to HTTPS.

A critical Android flaw could allow an attacker to run code on a phone without any user action remotely, Google said in its November security bulletin.

The flaw, CVE-2026-58868, affects Android 14 through 17. Phones get the fix with security patch level 2026-11-01 or later, which phone makers and carriers send on their own schedules.

As of November 4, Google's bulletin did not report any attacks exploiting its flaws. None of them was in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, kept by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, as of its November 3 update.

The flaw is a possible out-of-bounds write caused by a heap buffer overflow in the onOutputReceived function of the file FrameDecoder.cpp. Neither the bulletin nor the flaw's CVE record says how an attacker would reach that code.

Google's Critical rating assumes that the protections built into Android and Google's services are turned off or bypassed.

Older versions, such as Android 12 and 13, are not listed as affected by the flaw. Google's records do not say whether they contain it.

How to Check Your Phone

Google's help page gives these steps:

Open the Settings app.
Tap About phone, or About tablet, then Android version.
Find the dates for the Android security update and the Google Play system update.

The Android security update date is the phone's security patch level. A date of 2026-11-01 or later covers CVE-2026-58868 and the other flaws in the Framework, System, and Android runtime components.

A date of 2026-11-05 or later covers every flaw in the November bulletin, including those in the kernel and in parts from Arm, Imagination Technologies, MediaTek, Unisoc and Qualcomm.

Google sets two dates so phone makers can ship a set of fixes common to all Android devices sooner. It encourages them to include every fix in the bulletin.

Phones running Android 10 or later may also receive some fixes through Google Play system updates. This month's list for those updates includes another Critical flaw, CVE-2026-58876.

CVE-2026-58868 is not on that list, so the date to check for it is the Android security update.

The bulletin gives no workaround for phones that cannot install the update yet.

A Remote Denial-of-Service Flaw in Android's Text-Message Code

Another Critical flaw, CVE-2026-58882, could allow a remote denial-of-service attack with no user interaction, according to its CVE record. It is in decodeWapPdu, a function in Android's code for WAP Push messages that arrive via SMS.

On October 29, a researcher who publishes as Mark B posted a write-up called "SMS of Death" about a bug in the same function. Neither the bulletin nor the CVE record says whether CVE-2026-58882 is that bug.

One malformed WAP Push message crashes com.android.phone and ends any active call, including emergency calls, according to the write-up. In tests on several phone models, the crash happened every time.

The attacker needs only the target's phone number, and the message never shows up in the inbox. The phone retries the message each time it starts, so it can crash on startup until the message is removed.

A proof-of-concept app that sends such a message from one phone to another is public. Phones running Android 12 and 13 run the same code but do not receive the fix that newer versions do, the researcher says.

Other Critical Flaws

Google's November bulletin lists 216 vulnerabilities, 23 of them rated Critical. Two more Critical flaws could allow remote code execution: CVE-2026-58876 and CVE-2026-58936, both in Android's System component.

CVE-2026-122192: Guest Access to Firecracker Process Memory After a Failed Memory Discard

Bulletin ID: 2026-169-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 11/04/2026 11:30 AM PST

Description:

Firecracker is an open source virtualization technology that powers AWS Lambda and other serverless compute services. We identified CVE-2026-122192, an issue in Firecracker v0.23.0 through v1.16.1 that, under certain host memory conditions, can let a root user in a guest read or modify memory of the Firecracker process. It affects VMs restored from a snapshot using the File memory backend with a balloon or virtio-mem device.

AWS services including AWS Lambda are not affected by this issue. No customer action is required.

Impacted versions: Firecracker v0.23.0 through v1.16.1, inclusive.

Within the currently supported release lines, v1.16.0 and v1.16.1 are affected. The fix is included in v1.16.2 and v1.17.0

Resolution:

This issue is fixed in Firecracker v1.16.2 and v1.17.0. If you restore VMs using the File memory backend with a balloon or virtio-mem device, we recommend upgrading to Firecracker v1.16.2, v1.17.0 or later. Operators maintaining forks or derivative code should incorporate the corresponding fixes.

Workarounds:

If upgrading is not immediately possible, restore snapshots using the Uffd memory backend, following its documented requirements for handling discarded pages.

The following measures address known host-memory failure conditions:

On kernels without the Linux 6.12 overcommit-handling change, use heuristic overcommit (vm.overcommit_memory=0) and keep the maximum discard size no greater than the host’s total RAM plus swap.
Keep the memory cgroup’s out-of-memory (OOM) killer enabled.

These measures do not prevent every replacement-mapping failure.

References:

GHSA-48ww-rqpp-2mgm

title: SentinelOne Prompt Security: How the Console Fits Together
text: Before I get into the browser extension and the agent, I want to walk through the console itself. Almost every result later in this series - a key that got redacted, a key that sailed straight through, a pop-up that never showed - comes back to how four screens in the console work together. If you understand those four, the rest of the series makes sense. If you don't, half of it looks random.It took me a good few days of testing to get this picture straight, mostly because the console splits one decision across several places. So this part is the map I wish I'd had on day one.The four tabs, and how they connectEverything for employee AI use lives under one area with four tabs:Security Rules - who, which AI app, which platform, and what mode (watch, protect, block or ignore). The rule also picks which policy to use.Policies - what to look for in a prompt (secrets, personal data, your own patterns, topics) and what to do when it's found (redact or block).Sensor Settings - how the two pieces on the laptop behave: the browser extension and the endpoint agent.User Education - what the employee actually sees: warning pages, block messages, pop-ups.The way I explain it to people: the rule decides if and howthe policy decides whatthe sensor does the workthe user education does the talking. A prompt comes in, the first rule that matches decides the mode and hands it to a policy, the policy's detectors look at the text, and the sensor carries out the result.That split matters because a policy on its own does nothing. You can set "Block" on every detector in a policy, and if the rule that points to it is in Detect mode, nothing gets blocked. I fell for exactly that early on - the policy said block, the dashboard said 0% blocked, and it took a while to see why. Security RulesEach rule is one row with the same columns:Priority - rules are checked top-down and the first match wins. Nothing after it is looked at.Users - all users, named users (by e-mail), or groups once an identity provider is connected.Applications - one or more specific AI apps, a category, "All applications", or "AI code assistants". Several big apps come in two flavours, for example "ChatGPT (Personal)" and "ChatGPT (Enterprise)", so you can treat a personal account differently from the company one. The same goes for Claude, Gemini, Copilot and Perplexity.Platform - web (the browser extension) and/or desktop apps (the agent), with a count of how many desktop apps the rule covers.Mode - what happens (below), plus the policy it uses.Advanced - three drop-downs: Data protection, Logging and User education.At the bottom sit two rules you can't move or delete. The Default rule (All users / All applications / Detect / Default Employees Policy) catches everyone who didn't match anything above it. Just above it is a second locked rule for AI code assistants (All users / Detect / Default Developers Policy). Their users and apps fields carry a lock icon, so you can change the mode and the advanced settings but not who or what they apply to.The four modesModeWhat it doesDetectInspects the prompt, logs violations, can show a pop-up - but lets the prompt through untouchedProtectInspects and applies the policy's action: redact the sensitive part, or block the promptBlockBlocks the app outright, without reading the contentDon't TrackNo inspection, no logging, for that user and appDetect is visibility only. The AI gets the data and will happily repeat it back. If you want something to actually stop, you need Protect (or Block).What hides under "Advanced"This is the part of the rule screen I'd tell everyone to open, because the main row doesn't show it:Data protection - block content paste, block file upload, inspect uploaded files, block file download.Logging - log all interactions, or log only violations. Logging of AI replies is also set here, per rule.User education - whether to show the violations pop-up and the warning page for this rule.My very first test hit this. Pasting […]

title: Monitoring AI agent sessions: Leveraging embedding models to aid threat hunting and attack discovery workflows
text:
BlogMonitoring AI agent sessions: Leveraging embedding models to aid threat hunting and attack discovery workflowsI tested vector search on 7,454 turns of my own agent sessions. One in seven sessions needed review, the agent’s reasoning carried more signal than the prompt, and the stored vectors answer questions nobody thought to ask at ingest.November 04, 2026Marcus JeffesAI & AutomationThreat HuntingSOCJump to Share Query rules find behavior you can define, but agent sessions contain unstructured behaviors you can only describe. I stored six months of my own Claude Code and Cursor sessions as semantic vectors in Elastic and searched them instead of handing every session to a large language model (LLM). One in seven sessions came back requiring triage of suspicious actions. We can then create rules to detect semantically similar malicious chats and raise them to our security operations center (SOC). We now have a way to search across all agent sessions and to ask questions nobody thought to ask at ingest.Finding successful logins after multiple failed attempts is an easy query to make, because the log records every action a human decides to take, and we just have to query against known set fields to find conditions. AI agents break that model. A human describes an outcome, and the agent decides the actions. Every individual action can be allowed, while the session as a whole is a problem.AI agents could take on a large share of the operational work in a SOC, but adoption has been slower than the technology. A big part of that is trust. We have no scalable way to inspect what agents are doing beyond keyword and regex matching.The current answer is to have another model read every session. Uber’s Agentic AI Detection and Response (ADR) is the first production instance where I’ve seen this done well, but it costs money per session and the answers vary between runs. Plus, a new question means reevaluating everything already collected. That rules it out for threat hunting, where the job is asking new questions of old data.This article tests a different approach. I believe we need to go deeper in how we detect and the functions we use to detect this new attack vector. Each turn is embedded once at ingest and stored as vectors in Elastic. Hunting then becomes semantic search. You describe the behavior, or hand over a known bad session, and rank everything by similarity. Only what scores above a threshold goes to a human or an LLM.Why AI agent sessions are hard to detectAs an example of something hard to detect in agent chats, a developer asks their coding agent to tidy up a data export. The agent reads a CSV, which turns out to contain customer records. It runs git init, adds a remote repository, commits, and pushes to the repository. Every single action was allowed, so how do we find the security flaw? Reading a file in the project directory is allowed, and so is Git. The remote connection to github.com is also allowed, since half of engineering depends on it. Nothing alerts, because there was no rule made to detect this type of violation. We trust an AI coding assistant because it’s on our approved software list or can accomplish a task when prompted. We trust a remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool because IT likely installed it to help end users and it has a trusted signature. We even trust first-party applications to sign in on our behalf because the vendor ships them and our tenants pre-authorize them by default.But what happens when that foundation is flipped on its head?In this edition of the threats, etc quarterly report, drawn directly from confirmed customer intrusions and first-party research between April and September 2026, Elastic Security Threat Command observed that the things people were told to trust are now being used against them. Adversaries are no longer just trying to defeat our security mechanisms; they’re actively abusing the inherent trust we place in our enterprise stacks. 3 ways attackers abused trusted software Our report explores how adversaries are weaponizing legitimate tools and workflows. Three takeaways from this reporting window: Attackers are increasingly shifting away from traditional malware. Intrusions are now using signed, legitimate products, specifically remote monitoring agents, AI coding assistants, and Microsoft first-party clients, to maintain persistent, interactive access on contested endpoints. Out of 23 confirmed RMM abuse findings this quarter, ScreenConnect was the product named most often. Because these tools are inherently trusted, execution happens fast. In one confirmed healthcare finding, the behavior from a paste-and-run lure to Microsoft Software Installer (MSI) delivery with dynamic link library (DLL) sideloading took roughly 16 seconds. The speed of AI agent–driven attacksThreat actors are operating directly through AI applications. In one instance, an AI agent–driven attack resulted in roughly 17,600 reconstructed actions compressed into just four days: Victim consent is becoming a repeatable path for attackers to gain trusted access. By deploying Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) phishing kits and exploiting the gray areas of legacy authentication, attackers routinely bypass multifactor authentication (MFA) hurdles and use trusted applications to compromise cloud and software-as-a-service (SaaS) tenants. title: Application identity abuse targets MSPs and customer environments
text:
November 4, 2026

|

Security intelligence

Application identity abuse targets MSPs and customer environments

By Field Effect Security Intelligence Team

At a glance:

Threat actors are authenticating directly to Microsoft Entra ID and Azure DevOps using valid application credentials, allowing them to operate as trusted applications rather than compromised users.

MSPs appear to be a primary focus because applications used to manage customer environments can provide access across multiple tenants.

Review application credentials, workload identities, and multi-tenant applications for excessive permissions and cross-tenant access.

Threat summary
On November 3, 2026, researchers disclosed an ongoing intrusion campaign in which a threat actor used valid application credentials belonging to the victims' own applications to authenticate directly to Microsoft Entra ID and Azure DevOps environments.
The activity was first observed on November 1, 2026, and remained active as of November 3, with the latest observed attempt occurring at 21:31 UTC.
The activity is reported to primarily affect managed service providers (MSPs) and their customers, particularly those that rely on cloud apps, workload identities, and delegated administration across multiple tenants.
The threat actor signed in as trusted applications and replayed developer sessions, gaining whatever access those applications already held. How the adversary obtained these credentials remains under investigation. All confirmed malicious activity originated from a single IP address, 199.19.77[.]84, on a hosting provider geolocated to Poland.
Because applications sign in without a user, this activity sidesteps MFA and user-focused Conditional Access policies, and falls outside the view of on-premises firewalls. Conditional Access policies for applications offer partial protection, but they require an additional license and exclude the multi-tenant applications MSPs commonly rely on.
Once authenticated, the operator used application access to retrieve stored secrets and credentials. Previously unused applications often began authenticating within minutes, suggesting those secrets were used to expand access within affected environments. The adversary then searched and accessed mailboxes and file stores across multiple tenants, collecting files that contained credentials and configuration details for systems such as VPNs, remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools, backups, and firewalls.
The operator used MSP multi-tenant applications and Partner Center tokens to access customer environments. Researchers also observed attempts involving Granular Delegated Admin Privileges (GDAP) applications. Integration applications for security tools, including Todyl's own integration applications in two MSP tenants, were among the credentials abused, with no sign of a vendor platform compromise.
After detections fired on November 3, 2026, the adversary switched to spoofed browser signatures and later began replaying users' refresh tokens, while continuing to retry disabled and rotated applications in fixed 11-second loops. Conditional Access blocked every token replay observed that day.
Analysis
MSPs are the primary target of this campaign as the applications used to manage customer environments are designed to access multiple tenants, making them valuable to threat actors.
Application identities in particualr have become attractive targets because they often hold extensive permissions and operate with little day-to-day visibility. As organizations have strengthened protections around user accounts, threat actors have increasingly focused on applications, which commonly rely on long-lived credentials and maintain persistent access to cloud resources.

Barracuda patched two flaws that can be chained to give attackers root access to Email Security Gateway appliances.

How you export from ArcSight depends on which part of it holds the data. For history, search in ArcSight Logger and export the results. title: CVE-2026-119977: WordPress Core RCE Flaw Exploited During Software Upgrades
text:
En

CVEs

November 04, 2026
8 min read

A high-severity vulnerability in WordPress Core is being actively targeted in attacks, prompting the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to add the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. Tracked as CVE-2026-119977, the vulnerability carries a CVSS score of 8.1 and can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable server during a WordPress Core upgrade.

The vulnerability stems from a time-of-check time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition in the WordPress upgrade process. During full-package Core updates, WordPress temporarily stages installation files in predictable, web-accessible locations. Attackers can repeatedly probe these locations and attempt to reach installer components during the brief period in which an upgrade is taking place.

WordPress addressed the issue in version 7.1.4, released on October 28, 2026. The vulnerability affects WordPress versions 4.7 through 7.1.3, while security fixes have also been backported to eligible older branches. WordPress stresses that only the latest release is actively supported.

The risk has moved beyond theoretical exploitation. Wordfence telemetry cited by The Hacker News recorded more than 18,500 requests targeting staged setup-config.php installer paths during the first 21 hours after disclosure. CISA subsequently confirmed evidence of exploitation and required applicable U.S. federal civilian agencies to remediate the vulnerability by November 6, 2026.

Security teams can use the SOC Prime Platform to strengthen detection coverage against emerging exploitation techniques and hunt for suspicious activity associated with vulnerable internet-facing systems. Detect CVE-2026-119977 exploitation by monitoring abnormal requests to WordPress upgrade locations, unexpected PHP execution, newly created administrative accounts, suspicious files, and post-exploitation behavior.

Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added.

CVE-2026-119977 analysis

CVE-2026-119977 is classified as a TOCTOU race condition under CWE-367 and has a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1. Its vector reflects network-based exploitation requiring no privileges or user interaction, with high potential impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Attack complexity is rated high because successful exploitation depends on reaching a vulnerable resource during a narrow upgrade window.

CVE-2026-119977 affects WordPress Core releases from version 4.7 through 7.1.3. The weakness is not tied to a third-party plugin or theme; it exists in the Core software upgrade mechanism itself.

The issue occurs during full-package Core upgrades. WordPress temporarily extracts the new package into a staging location beneath the wp-content/upgrade directory before replacing the existing installation. In affected releases, portions of this staging location can be predictable and reachable from the web while the update is underway.

One particularly important component is the staged setup-config.php installer. An unauthenticated attacker who correctly predicts the temporary path and reaches that component before WordPress completes cleanup may be able to interact with the staged installation and ultimately execute PHP code on the server.

This creates an unusual exploitation model. A vulnerable WordPress site is not necessarily continuously exploitable. Instead, the attacker must catch the site during the brief period in which a full-package upgrade exposes the staging files. Researchers indicate that the opportunity may last only seconds.

Two Canada nationals face charges in the United States for hacking university supercomputers, stealing login credentials and mining cryptocurrency for financial gain. Canada extradited one of the suspects to the United States; federal prosecutors still seek custody of the other alleged hacker.See Also: OnDemand | 2024 Phishing Insights: What 11.9 Million User Behaviors Reveal About Your Risk
Ryan James Roach, 35, of Saskatchewan, and Mathiew James Stubbings, 41, of Ontario, are charged with three counts of offenses: conspiracy to obtain information from and cause damage to a protected computer, obtaining information from a protected computer and intentional damage to a protected computer.

Roach appeared in U.S. district court on Oct. 28 following his arrest and remains in custody pending a detention hearing, the Department of Justice said Tuesday. Stubbings' extradition proceedings are ongoing.

A recently unsealed indictment alleges that the defendants exploited vulnerabilities in their targets' computer networks to gain unauthorized access between June 2016 and December 2019. Victims included educational institutions in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina and Massachusetts.

To conceal their identities, the defendants rented virtual private servers from bulletproof hosts in Europe and the United States under false names. They also used compromised computers from another victim.

Once inside the victim environments, the defendants conducted reconnaissance, expanded their access within the networks and established command-and-control connections. They deployed malware on victims' computers to steal credentials and exfiltrate data.

The defendants also sent cryptocurrency mining software to the high-performance computers. Investigators said at least one supercomputer mined cryptocurrency Electroneum on the defendants' behalf, draining so much computing power that the machine became unavailable to the research institution.

"As a result of the scheme, the Defendants damaged ten or more protected computers during a one-year period," says the indictment. "The Defendants also caused an aggregate loss of at least $5,000 to persons during a one-year period, resulting from a related course of conduct that affected one or more other protected computers."

The charges carry a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

(Image: Shutterstock)
Cybersecurity skills always grow when we practice with evidence connected to real systems. That was my clearest lesson from a recent three-day capture-the-flag exercise hosted by Dragos focused largely on blue-team forensics, network analysis and operational technology.See Also: What If Your Security Licensing Could Adapt to Your Cloud?
I have participated in several CTFs, including the National Cyber League and MetaCTF. The Dragos annual exercise felt different because the challenges had a context that is fundamentally alien to those who have no experience working in operational technology. Though much of the work involved more common techniques such as Wireshark PCAP analysis, the context of the analysis contributed to the difficulty
That distinction matters. In a traditional cybersecurity CTF, many experienced practitioners already understand the protocols, file formats and tools in front of them. OT changes the equation. Someone can know cybersecurity well and still have little experience with the protocols and devices used in industrial environments.
Modbus is a good example. A security practitioner may understand networking, packet analysis and lateral movement but have little reason to encounter Modbus in daily work. In OT, it may be central to understanding how controllers and other devices communicate.
The technical evidence only becomes useful when you understand its context.
The Hard Part Is Understanding the Story
The Dragos CTF included multiple scenarios involving environments such as utilities, water systems and power facilities. Participants received network traffic and other artifacts, then had to find flags by analyzing the evidence locally.
Wireshark was one of the tools I used throughout the event. The challenges exposed me to Modbus/TCP, BACnet, HTTP authentication, SMB and SSH. I also used CyberChef to decode data and Impacket to examine a provided Windows SAM database.
But using a tool is not the same as understanding what its output means.
A Modbus register write becomes more significant when you know which controller received it, what equipment the controller affects and where the activity fits in the attack sequence. A packet capture is not just a collection of packets. It is a partial record of a story.
One useful artifact was a hand-drawn network diagram connecting remote access and supporting systems to a Wonderware HMI, PLCs and other devices. The diagram helped turn individual packets into an attack path.
That is the type of context defenders need during an actual investigation. They have to determine what happened, how the attacker moved and what the activity meant to the environment.
OT makes that reasoning especially important because technical actions can have physical consequences. But the broader lesson applies outside industrial environments. Every organization has systems with dependencies, business purposes and operating requirements. Investigators make better decisions when they understand those relationships before interpreting the evidence.
A Beginner and an Expert See Different Problems
The exercise also reinforced how differently beginners and experienced practitioners approach the same evidence.
For someone with experience, opening a PCAP file may feel trivial. A beginner may not know what a PCAP file is, which program can open it or what information inside matters.
That gap is easy to overlook when we teach cybersecurity.

Bots Getting Better at Hacking Operational Technology
Artificial Intelligence Needs Human Help to Hack OT - For Now

Shaun Waterman •
November 4, 2026

$('.fa.fa-print').click(function () {
window.print();
});

Image: Shutterstock

A fully AI-powered hack against OT today is still a fantasy, the breathless stuff of hype, according to many experts. But how long will it stay that way?See Also: Frictionless Security: How AI is Redefining Access in Highly Regulated Industries
Two research teams using very different testing methodologies and a different selection of models have shown the advanced artificial intelligence models can more-or-less reliably, and with some human guidance, autonomously execute each separate step in a multi-stage attack chain in an unfamiliar OT network - though the attacks are often inefficient and noisy.
The skill of the operator writing prompts and providing guidance is a big factor. At the very least, large language models and their agents have succeeded in collapsing the barrier to entry-level industrial control systems hacking once required specialist skills and training.
"Specialized OT knowledge, unfamiliar equipment, and complex control environments are no longer meaningful barriers to attack," reads one of the two research reports, from technology services giant Booz Allen Hamilton. BAH researchers used AI agents built around LLMs from the two leading frontier labs, Anthropic and OpenAI, and tested them in a special OT lab set-up.
Human guidance in the attack decision loop will be a requirement "for the near future," said Harry Thomas cofounder and CTO of Frenos, which tested a variety of frontier and open weight models in a sort of written exam where they asked the LLMs to explain how they would hack OT systems. "Full autonomy still requires a capable [agentic] harness to support these AI models, and … unattended execution of AI attacks could be noisy," said Thomas.
In an OT environment, mistakes can easily alert defenders. "I used to be a hacker, right? When I made a mistake inside an OT environment, the SOAR and incident response definitely let me know that they found me," he said, referring to security orchestration and automated response systems.
The level of human skill required varies depending on the model, said Thomas.
"With the open weight models we're seeing, I believe you would have to be pretty capable and knowledgeable to get enough use out of those to continue your attack chain." Frontier models were capable of being successful with less expert input, Thomas explained.
Critical infrastructure at greater risk
AI enabled cyberattacks will "likely put critical infrastructure at greater risk just because it lowers the bar to entry," said Rob Bair, principal industry advisor, cybersecurity, for frontier lab Anthropic. He also spoke at the launch of the Frenos report. And, he added, "The models are getting better and better."
An unsophisticated attacker might be able to do "a little research online and understand how a water plant works," at least well enough to give feedback to an LLM, said Paul Shaver, head of OT for Armadin.
As OT security firm Dragos CEO Rob Lee noted recently of life-critical service providers like water and power utilities, "AI will make it faster for adversaries to find these facilities, identify their OT, and start operations against them."

U.S. District Judge William Orrick of the Northern District of California on Oct. 30 granted certification to four classes of Facebook users in multidistrict consolidated litigation. The lawsuit accuses Meta of intercepting patients' confidential communications with healthcare providers and prescription drug websites, apps and portals through its Meta Pixel and other online tracking technologies.
The class certification represents a significant procedural victory for the plaintiffs, who contend that Meta acquired though the use of its Pixel and other tracking tools sensitive information about patients' medical conditions, treatments, prescriptions and interactions with healthcare providers without their knowledge or consent.
"I'm not surprised that four classes were certified. Class actions are made for situations like this," said regulatory attorney Lucia Savage, former chief privacy officer at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT during the Obama administration.
"It's to be determined if the plaintiffs will win overall, but the scope of this Meta case could be a game-changer for internet based marketing," Savage said.
The certification allows the plaintiffs to pursue their litigation on behalf of potentially millions of similarly situated individuals, who seek monetary damages and injunctive relief, such as restrictions on how Meta collects and uses sensitive healthcare information.
Orrick's ruling allows patients to pursue six categories of legal claims against Meta, including alleged violations of federal and California electronic privacy laws, breach of contract, intrusion upon seclusion and unauthorized computer access.
The four court-certified classes of Facebook users include individuals whose healthcare-related information or online activities were allegedly collected by Meta beginning June 17, 2018, to the present.

In January, after several years away from 1Password, I resumed using it at work and also began migrating my family from Bitwarden to 1Password Families. I decided to move my family to 1Password because Bitwarden has gotten extraordinarily buggy. Based on past experience with 1Password, I thought it would be better.

I may have been wrong. Since I’ve resumed using 1Password, I’ve encountered a lot of significant issues. I initially kept a running tally of them in a Mastodon thread. However, since then I’ve decided to start auto-deleting my Mastodon posts after a year, so that thread is eventually going to disappear. I think my experience with 1Password is worth preserving for the benefit of anyone else who might be considering using 1Password and wants to know what they’re getting into. Therefore, I am back-filling the contents of that thread into this post, and moving forward if I encounter any additional issues I will record them both here and in that thread.

January 17, 2026

1Password’s SSO implementation, which we’re using at work to integrate 1Password login with Okta, is immature and has a lot of UX issues. Generally speaking, it does not appear to be particularly robust from a UX point of view (I have no reason to doubt it’s robustness security-wise.

For example: if you try to log into 1Password via SSO on a new device, it’s supposed to display a prompt on existing devices to approve the login. However, if you have a linked personal account that’s unlocked while your work account is locked, you won’t see the prompt or any instructions for how to retrieve it until it occurs to you to unlock your work account. This is shitty UX.

January 17, 2026

1Password is integrated with only one email masking service, Fastmail. In contrast, Bitwarden has integrations with numerous services, including the one I use, Addy.io. Until 1Password gets around to adding an integration with Addy.io (which I’m not holding my breath for; people have been asking for this for a while), I guess I have to use the separate Addy.io extension for this. Definitely not a great UX.

In contrast, Bitwarden supports integrations with a number of email masking services, including Addy.io.

January 17, 2026

There’s no way to tell the 1Password browser extension not to prompt to save passwords on a particular website. Again, I’m not holding my breath that they’re going to fix this any time soon because people have been asking for it for a long time. This is another area where 1Password lags behind Bitwarden.

January 17, 2026

Significant bug: the 1Password CLI allows you to retrieve items as JSON using the item title or unique ID. You’re supposed to be able to then edit it and upload the edited JSON via the CLI to save the changes. However, when you retrieve an item from your “Private” vault using its title instead of its ID, the resulting JSON file calls the vault “Personal” rather than “Private”, and then when you try to upload the changes the JSON is rejected because of the vault name mismatch.

January 21, 2026

1Password support says they are unable to reproduce this issue. I have responded with a Python script that demonstrates the issue by calling the 1Password CLI, along with the output I see when I run that script to show that I have described the behavior accurately.

January 17, 2026

The 1Password desktop app has robust export functionality, which I’m pretty sure is new since my last stint using 1Password.

Good for them for adding this! Data portability is important.

Unfortunately, it’s only available in the app, not in the browser extension or on the website.

More unfortunately (significant bug), it doesn’t appear to work on Linux. The export command is there, but when I enter my password and click the button to do the export, nothing happens.

It works fine on macOS.

82,478 Rows and a Google Drive Folder: How One C2 Server Pulled Data From Mexican Organizations

There’s no custom implant or polished framework in this story. The operator behind this C2 environment used a 30-line Python HTTP server, a few XML files, an SSH tunnel and a separate dump script for each target. All of the stolen data went to a Google Drive remote named leviathan-drive.In late October 2026, that setup was pointed at five organizations in Mexico: two telecom providers, an insurance platform, a state government and a public university. In our C2 Environment and Targeted Data Extraction report, ThreatMon’s threat intelligence team reconstructed how it worked from the server’s own scripts and logs.

Key Findings

The environment held separate, purpose-built extraction scripts for five Mexican targets: two telecom providers, one insurance provider, one government entity and one university. Victim names are anonymized in the report.The logs record completed extraction and cloud sync for three of them: 82,478 SIM-related rows from Telecom Provider A, 306 invoice records from Telecom Provider B and 554 records from the insurance platform.Access appears to start with malicious XML payloads run through Java’s ProcessBuilder, followed by a reverse SSH tunnel that exposes internal Oracle databases (TCP/1521).Data left in compressed .jsonl.gz files through rclone to Google Drive, and local copies were deleted after each upload.The server also stored WebLogic configuration, encrypted DB credentials and an ED25519 SSH private key. These remain a risk if they’re still valid.Initial access, the operator’s identity and the full volume of exfiltrated data were not established.

How the Operation Fits Together

The tooling isn’t one C2 framework. It’s a kit of small tools, one per stage. The report’s reconstruction of the chain looks like this:Intrusion chain observed in the campaignExecution. Four XML files carry Java and Spring constructs that run shell commands. bridge.xml uses ProcessBuilder to download run_bridge.sh from 34.66.239.213 and run it. recon.xml and check_tools.xml map the host. payload.xml tries to bundle WebLogic config and credential files. These files point to an exposed Java/WebLogic application as the entry point, but we couldn’t tie them to a specific CVE.Tunneling. run_bridge.sh downloads an SSH key and wls_bridge.py. The bridge then reads its endpoints from remote JSON config and opens a reverse tunnel that forwards port 1521. title: A Typo, a Leaked Token and Booby-Trapped Go Packages: Inside the CCDS C2 Server
text:
Blog

October 28, 2026

Stealer & Malware

Summarize with:

A Typo, a Leaked Token and Booby-Trapped Go Packages: Inside the CCDS C2 Server

The CCDS controller crashed on a single misspelled exception name. Its own logs then printed the full source path, the function names and the line numbers of the code that failed. It’s an unusual way to learn how a C2 framework works, but that’s how much of this analysis came together.In our CCDS C2: Infrastructure and Payload Analysis report, ThreatMon’s threat intelligence team looked at artifacts recovered from 161.97.113.228, a Debian VPS running a custom remote-control framework its developer calls CCDS. The same server also hosted a set of Go packages that open a reverse shell or send system data the moment another project imports them. That second part is the one software teams should pay attention to.

Key Findings

CCDS is a custom, Python-based C2 framework for Linux. It supports remote shell execution, agent management and two-way file transfer, with size and hash checks on every transfer.Two communication models were found. One is a persistent TLS listener on TCP/4444 with a local management API. The other is an HTTP(S) polling agent that checked auto.0xnayel.com every second.The controller ran as an enabled systemd service, ccds-c2.service, so it survived restarts.Authentication relied on one shared REVSHELL_TOKEN. A full copy of the token sat in plaintext in archived session data.Go packages on the same server use init() functions and a CGO constructor to launch a Bash reverse shell or exfiltrate data to TCP/9999 as soon as they’re loaded.The logs date the activity to 13–14 June 2026. They show testing and discovery only. No destructive commands, victims or attribution were found.

What CCDS Does

The TLS version keeps operator traffic and agent traffic apart. The operator sends commands to a management API bound to 127.0.0.1:5001 (POST /execute, GET /agents). The controller then forwards them over a persistent TLS session to agents connected on 0.0.0.0:4444.CCDS controller communication architectureThe first agent, kali-1, registered about 31 seconds after the controller started. Its first command was echo "alive" && uname -r. Next came a round of file transfer tests: 100 KB and 2 MB files were uploaded to /tmp, pulled back and compared by hash. The controller also retrieved /etc/hostname, which shows it can collect files already on the host and isn’t limited to files it placed there.The other commands in the logs were standard reconnaissance: whoami, id, uname -a, reading /etc/os-release, and a curl call to api.ipify.org to learn the agent’s public IP. Nothing destructive appears. The agent still accepts any shell string it’s given, though, so this is a general-purpose remote shell, not a limited admin tool.The polling agent test-agent-1 handled file operations a little differently. It used reserved prefixes, __file_read__ and __file_write__, and attached an eight-character job ID to each task. One test file was named agent-secret.txt, but it only contained the string “this is a secret payload” followed by a Unix timestamp. That timestamp is how we dated an otherwise undated log to 14 June 2026.

The Mistakes That Gave It Away

A misspelled exception. The controller’s error handler catches ssl.SSLErrorWantReadError. Python has no such class; the correct name is ssl.SSLWantReadError. When an agent connection broke, Python tried to evaluate that name, raised an AttributeError and wrote a full traceback to the log. The traceback showed the controller’s internal flow from do_POST() to _read_result(), along with file paths and line numbers. For hunters, it also works as a fingerprint for this specific codebase.A port open to the internet. Because 4444 was bound to every interface, internet scanners found it within hours. text:
Mara Sugue reports:
Lab 1 has published a report analysing 328 million files from 2,089 datasets exposed after cyber attacks. It found that the median breach now exposes data linked to 542 organisations beyond the named victim.
The study also found that 13,436 unique organisations were exposed through incidents recorded between 2025 and 2026, underlining how stolen data can affect companies that were not the direct target of an intrusion.
The findings are based on what Lab 1 described as the largest published content-level review of stolen datasets posted online after breaches. The report examined files taken in attacks and assessed the types of information they contained, including material in emails, PDFs and other unstructured documents.

Key takeaways

Ryohin Keikaku, which runs MUJI, said on October 30 that email addresses, birth dates and gender of up to 27.26 million MUJI app users may have leaked, and that card details, names and addresses were not included.
Its second report on November 4 changed that. The 27.26 million also covers online store customers, about 520,000 of them with names, addresses and phone numbers, and the attackers may have reached full card numbers of about 1.09 million MUJI Card credit cards, about 345,000 of them still valid.
The card numbers came from the card's issuer, Credit Saison, which passed them to MUJI from 2000 to July 2021 so that MUJI could give points for card use. MUJI changed the scheme in 2021, but the numbers stayed in its systems.
No holder names, expiry dates or security codes were included. But for about 168,000 valid cards, the numbers sat alongside the holders' email addresses and birth dates, and for about 25,000, alongside names and addresses.
The attack began around 01:00 on October 29, according to Credit Saison. MUJI has still not said how the attackers got in.

According to Credit Saison, a third party gained unauthorized access to Ryohin Keikaku's systems at around 01:00 on October 29. "We discovered that an unauthorized third party accessed the server that runs our web-based File Manager at files.dreamhost.com," DreamHost wrote in its notification, describing a breach that ran from August 2026 until October 23, 2026.

DreamHost's account of the intrusion
DreamHost has confirmed attackers gained access to its File Manager platform and stole FTP/SFTP credentials for users who logged into that web-based tool during the window from approximately August 2026 through October 23, 2026 — the day the company says it discovered the activity. In its data breach notification the company said an "unauthorized third party exploited a vulnerability in that software" to obtain the usernames and passwords.
The notification also says the intruder may have accessed webmail systems, exposing session information and credentials for a limited number of users. DreamHost described the attack as deliberate and said its staff has been working nonstop to contain it.

Data types exposed: FTP/SFTP logins and webmail sessions
According to the notification, the primary data confirmed as exposed were FTP and SFTP usernames and passwords for individuals who used the File Manager at files.dreamhost.com during the affected period. Separately, DreamHost cautioned that session information — including credentials — for a limited number of webmail users may also have been exposed.
The company reported it has "found no evidence" that the attacker accessed control panel login information or customer billing and payment details; billing and payment data are handled by an external provider, DreamHost added.

They use words like "anomaly" or "unauthorised access event," as if the attackers simply walked through the front door because they forgot to lock it, rather than exploiting a systemic collapse of trust in the supply chain.

The story of the week is OpsShield. For those who don't follow the minutiae of server management tools, OpsShield provides cPGuard. It’s designed to keep servers secure. The irony, which I suspect will be lost on the regulators in Brussels, is that the very mechanism used to push security updates was hijacked.

The attackers didn't have to find a hole in the perimeter; they were invited in via the official update channel. Just under 3,000 servers were served malicious updates. That’s not a breach in the traditional sense—it's a betrayal of the delivery pipeline. When you compromise the update server, you aren't just hitting one target; you're using the vendor's own reputation as a Trojan horse.

We have spent a decade preaching the gospel of "patch early, patch often." We’ve built an entire industry around reducing the window between disclosure and remediation. But we’ve ignored the second-order effect: by automating the patching process to a fever pitch, we've created a high-speed delivery system for malware if that pipeline is ever compromised.

The strongest objection here, usually from the vendor side, is that manual verification of every binary update is impossible at scale. They’re right. You cannot ask a sysadmin to reverse-engineer a proprietary update before clicking "install." But this brings us to the actual problem: liability. Currently, the burden of risk sits almost entirely with the end user. If OpsShield pushes a backdoor, the 2,950 affected servers suffer the data theft, while the vendor issues a polite apology and a new patch. We are operating on a trust model that has been thoroughly debunked. Until we have mandatory software bills of materials (SBOMs) that actually mean something—and legal frameworks where vendors are financially responsible for "signed" malicious code—we are just speeding up the rate at which we get infected.

Then there is the matter of France’s blood stocks. This feels like a grim sequel to the supermarket refrigeration attacks I've been tracking. In those cases, the loss was commercial—spoilt frozen peas and ice cream. Here, attackers pushed freezer settings from -22F up to 230F.

Moving a temperature that drastically isn't just about stealing data; it’s about destroying physical assets. It is an act of sabotage. The machinery of regulation usually moves slowly because it’s trying to protect "data," which is an abstract concept. But when the target is blood viability, the timeline changes. I suspect the French authorities will find that their current reporting requirements are woefully inadequate for "kinetic" cyber attacks. A 72-hour notification window under GDPR is useless when your blood supply has been cooked in a freezer.

***

**MAILBAG**

**Gary, Leeds: "I’m running cPGuard on several client boxes. I saw the news about the OpsShield updates. Should I just disable auto-updates entirely and wait for a manual confirmation from the vendor?"**

Gary, I understand the impulse to hit the big red switch. However, disabling auto-updates is often just trading one risk for another. If you stop updating, you're simply waiting for someone to exploit a known CVE that you’ve ignored.

The real question is: how are you monitoring your servers for anomalous behaviour *after* an update? If you can't verify the binary, you have to verify the behavior. Watch your outbound traffic and look for new, unexplained processes. […]

Lab 1 warns breach data now exposes thousands more firms

Thu, 5th Nov 2026 (Today)

MARA SUGUE

News Editor

Lab 1 has published a report analysing 328 million files from 2,089 datasets exposed after cyber attacks. It found that the median breach now exposes data linked to 542 organisations beyond the named victim.

The study also found that 13,436 unique organisations were exposed through incidents recorded between 2025 and 2026, underlining how stolen data can affect companies that were not the direct target of an intrusion.

The findings are based on what Lab 1 described as the largest published content-level review of stolen datasets posted online after breaches. The report examined files taken in attacks and assessed the types of information they contained, including material in emails, PDFs and other unstructured documents.

It found that 44% of the files reviewed, or about 145 million documents, contained financial information. This included banking details, tax identifiers, invoicing records and other documents that could be used in invoice fraud, payment redirection scams, impersonation and resale on criminal marketplaces.

A further 29 million files, or 9% of the total, contained human resources information. These records included personally identifiable information, payroll documents, employment contracts and identity papers, which could be used in phishing, synthetic identity fraud, deepfake material and voice-cloning attempts.

Less common but more sensitive forms of exposure also appeared in the data. Private cryptographic keys were found in about 15% of the incidents analysed, pointing to the risk of attackers using breach material to gain access to systems, bypass authentication controls and widen their reach inside affected organisations.

Supply-chain reach

The report argues that the effects of a breach often extend well beyond the organisation named in public reporting. For technology, information and internet companies, the median number of additional organisations exposed in breaches dating from 2022 onwards was 6,985, the highest among the sectors reviewed.

That pattern reflects the central role those businesses play in supply chains and data-sharing arrangements with customers, suppliers, users and partners. In a sample of 130 incidents linked to 17 groups that launched or set up new data-leak sites over a one-year period, Lab 1 identified about 950,000 organisational exposures, including roughly 71,000 supply-chain organisations.

The volume of breach material is also rising. Newly added incidents in the enlarged dataset had a median size of 29.8 GB, up 121.7% from 13.44 GB in the previous study, while the median number of files rose 44.5% to 32,734 from 22,647.

AI analysis

Lab 1 said threat actors are becoming more systematic in how they examine stolen data. It identified seven threat actor groups conducting structured analysis of breached data, compared with one in 2024.

The report described several cases in which criminal groups claimed to have used artificial intelligence tools to search and classify large collections of stolen documents. In one example, a group known as FulcrumSec said it had searched a 400,000-email archive and isolated 61 emails linked to engagements with US-sanctioned entities for use in pressure tactics against the victim.

In another example cited in the report, the same group claimed to have used AI agents to review 700,717 breached files and identify 11,500 patient records across named clinical trials, 41,144 proprietary compound structures, 32 private AI models and five undisclosed drug programmes.

Lab 1 also said it had observed what it described as the first indexing-as-a-service offering for cyber criminals, designed to sort stolen data into categories that can be monetised.
