# Someone Forgot to Close the Freezer

The most alarming report on my desk this evening isn't about stolen credit cards or leaked passwords, but about thermodynamics.

In France, attackers managed to get inside the control systems for critical blood stocks and didn't just steal data—they changed the thermostat. They pushed freezer settings from -22F up to 230F. It is a brutal piece of work because it targets the viability of the product itself. If you ruin the blood, the data doesn't matter; the patients do.

This is a textbook example of setpoint manipulation. In industrial control systems (ICS), a setpoint is the target value that a controller tries to maintain. The system isn't "broken" in the traditional sense; it's doing exactly what it was told to do. It saw the new target—230F—and worked diligently to heat the freezers to reach that goal. This is far more insidious than a simple crash or a lockout. The system remains operational, but its purpose has been inverted.

This rhymes with Stuxnet in 2010, where attackers manipulated the frequency converters of centrifuges to make them spin at unstable speeds. Both cases use the legitimate logic of the machine against itself. Where the parallel breaks down is in the intent. Stuxnet was a masterpiece of stealth designed to delay a program for years without being noticed. This attack on France's medical infrastructure is loud, destructive, and immediate. It isn't about subtlety; it's about spoilage.

My confidence level regarding attribution here is low. While some are quick to point toward state actors given the criticality of blood supplies, we have no forensic evidence linking this to a specific group's infrastructure. To move my confidence to moderate, I would need to see the specific malware used to override the setpoints or a leak from a known actor claiming responsibility. Until then, it could just as easily be an opportunistic ransomware group that stumbled into a PLC they didn't understand and accidentally triggered a catastrophe.

It is a terrifying prospect because we are seeing a trend where attackers stop caring about the data and start caring about the physical state of the world.

Then we have the OpsShield situation. This one is a more traditional, though no less severe, supply chain failure. Attackers compromised the update infrastructure to serve malicious cPGuard updates to approximately 2,950 servers. Once the "update" landed, it deployed a backdoor and started exfiltrating data.

The tradecraft here relies on the trust anchor paradox. We are told that automated updates are the only way to keep a perimeter secure in real-time. Therefore, we grant update mechanisms high privileges and often exempt them from rigorous inspection because they are the "trusted" source of truth. Attackers simply move their point of entry upstream. They don't have to break into 2,950 servers individually; they just have to break into one server that those 2,950 machines already trust implicitly.

I have moderate confidence that this was a targeted operation rather than a random botnet infection, given the specific targeting of the update pipeline. However, I distrust the rush to name a particular APT. Supply chain attacks are often mirrored; one group discovers the hole and sells the access to three others. If we see similar backdoors appearing in different sectors using the same OpsShield vector, that would shift my confidence toward a broader criminal enterprise rather than a single nation-state mission.

The second-order effect here is the "update freeze." Whenever a major update mechanism is weaponized, cautious sysadmins stop updating everything. They move to manual verification or just stop patching altogether for a few weeks. Quantique : le risque industriel que les investisseurs ne peuvent plus ignorer [Partie 1/2]

Jonathan Chaste

Publié le
04/11/2026

Analyse

Le calcul quantique attire les États et les investisseurs. Mais avant de tenir ses promesses, chaque machine doit être fabriquée avec des matériaux très purs, produits par peu d’acteurs et parfois par un seul. Ce risque industriel reste peu présent dans les analyses d’investissement. L’intelligence économique permet de le repérer à temps.

Un ordinateur classique traite l’information sous forme de bits, qui valent 0 ou 1. Un ordinateur quantique utilise des qubits, qui exploitent les lois de la matière à l’échelle de l’atome. Il ne remplacera pas nos ordinateurs. Il vise à régler certains problèmes que les machines actuelles ne savent pas résoudre en un temps raisonnable. Trois usages concentrent les attentes:

La chimie et la santé. Simuler des molécules pour concevoir de nouveaux médicaments ou matériaux.

La sécurité. À terme, un ordinateur quantique pourrait casser une partie du chiffrement, dit à clé publique, qui protège aujourd’hui les communications bancaires, diplomatiques et militaires. À l’inverse, les mêmes principes permettent de mieux sécuriser les communications.

La mesure. Des capteurs d’une précision inédite, utiles à la défense comme à la navigation.

Le quantique est donc devenu un enjeu de souveraineté. Le pays qui maîtrisera ces technologies pourrait disposer d’un avantage durable, notamment en matière de sécurité. Celui qui en dépendra devra s’en remettre à d’autres. Les États-Unis, la Chine et l’Europe investissent donc pour passer du laboratoire à l’industrie. Adoptée en juillet 2025, la stratégie Quantum Europe de la Commission européenne vise ainsi à faire de l’Europe un acteur mondial de premier plan d’ici 2030, en renforçant son industrie et en sécurisant ses chaînes d’approvisionnement.

Or passer à l’industrie suppose de fabriquer ces machines, et donc de disposer des bons matériaux au bon moment. Le silicium 28, est un matériau clé pour certains ordinateurs quantiques. En mars 2025, l’entreprise américaine ASP Isotopes annonçait le démarrage de son usine d’enrichissement de silicium 28, à Koedoespoort, près de Pretoria, en Afrique du Sud. Les premières livraisons commerciales étaient attendues le trimestre suivant. En août 2026, elles n’avaient toujours pas commencé.

Pour un investisseur, la question devient concrète. Une entreprise quantique peut-elle tenir son calendrier si un matériau, un fournisseur spécialisé ou une usine indispensable vient à manquer ? Ce risque est moins visible que les performances, les brevets ou les perspectives commerciales. Il peut pourtant retarder la fabrication, augmenter les besoins de financement et peser sur la valeur d’un investissement.C’est l’un des rôles de l’intelligence économique, car la veille et l’analyse des chaînes d’approvisionnement permettent de repérer ces dépendances avant qu’elles ne pèsent sur l’entreprise.

De la promesse scientifique au risque industriel

Analyser une entreprise quantique, c’est d’abord examiner sa technologie, ses performances, ses brevets, son équipe et ses marchés. Mais une technologie prometteuse ne fait pas une entreprise viable. Encore faut-il pouvoir la fabriquer, dans les délais et au coût que suppose son modèle économique.

Or il n’existe pas un ordinateur quantique, mais plusieurs familles technologiques, appelées architectures. Toutes reposent sur le qubit, l’équivalent quantique du bit. Mais chacune le fabrique à sa manière, avec ses propres matériaux et ses propres fournisseurs.

Les qubits supraconducteurs sont des circuits électriques gravés dans des métaux qui, une fois refroidis, conduisent le courant sans aucune résistance. Ils fonctionnent à quelques centièmes de degré, voire moins, au-dessus du zéro absolu (environ -273 °C), pour que l’agitation thermique ne détruise pas l’information. Quantique : le risque industriel que les investisseurs ne peuvent plus ignorer [Partie 2/2]

Jonathan Chaste

Publié le
04/11/2026

Analyse

Le silicium 28, un exemple des difficultés du passage à l’échelle

Le silicium est l’un des éléments les plus abondants de la croûte terrestre. Mais toutes ses formes ne se valent pas. Le silicium naturel mélange trois variantes du même atome, appelées isotopes. Environ 4,7 % de ces atomes, ceux de silicium 29, se comportent comme de minuscules aimants. Ils perturbent les qubits de spin et leur font perdre l’information qu’ils portent, un phénomène appelé décohérence.

En retirant ces atomes pour ne garder presque que du silicium 28, ce qu’on appelle l’enrichissement, les qubits conservent leur information plus longtemps. Ils peuvent donc enchaîner davantage d’opérations avant de commettre une erreur.

Le défi n’est donc pas d’accéder au silicium. Il est de produire un matériau assez pur, d’atteindre les exigences des fabricants et de l’intégrer dans les plaquettes sur lesquelles les puces sont gravées.

Le parcours d’ASP Isotopes illustre une distinction essentielle; celle qui sépare une capacité annoncée d’une production réellement qualifiée et vendue. Prévues pour le deuxième trimestre 2025, les livraisons ont d’abord été repoussées à août 2025, pour un produit enrichi à au moins 99,995 %. La société a alors expédié des premiers échantillons à des clients.

L’échéance a ensuite glissé au deuxième trimestre 2026, puis au troisième, après des modifications techniques de l’installation. En août 2026, la société a de nouveau repoussé ses livraisons au second de la même année. Et ce premier lot ne sera enrichi qu’à 99 %. Pour atteindre les 99,995 % généralement exigés par le quantique, l’usine devra encore ajouter des étages d’enrichissement. Fin octobre 2026, aucune livraison commerciale de silicium 28 n’avait été annoncée.

Toutes ces dates figurent dans des documents publics. Les suivre, c’est déjà faire de la veille. Elles ne prouvent pas qu’une entreprise quantique donnée dépend d’ASP Isotopes. Elles révèlent surtout un écart fréquent dans l’industrie, entre l’annonce d’une usine et la livraison d’un produit qualifié, en quantité suffisante, néanmoins le chemin est souvent long.

Pour un fabricant de qubits, ces étapes s’enchaînent : approvisionnement en silicium enrichi; fabrication de la plaquette; gravure du circuit; puis validation du dispositif. Un retard en amont se répercute sur toute la chaîne. Cela peut imposer des essais supplémentaires, ainsi décaler la validation industrielle et repousser les premières ventes.

La souveraineté se joue sur toute la chaîne d’approvisionnement

Ce mécanisme prend une dimension géopolitique quand une technologie dépend d’usines concentrées dans quelques pays ou chez quelques acteurs. Être souverain, ce n’est pas seulement concevoir une technologie sur son territoire. C’est pouvoir accéder aux matériaux, aux équipements et aux procédés nécessaires pour la fabriquer, y compris quand le contexte commercial ou international se dégrade.

La photonique en offre un exemple européen. De plus en plus de puces photoniques utilisent du niobate de lithium en couche mince, un cristal capable de moduler la lumière très rapidement. Or, comme le relevait le CEA-Leti en juin 2025, l’Europe dépendait jusque-là d’un seul fournisseur commercial de ce matériau, situé hors de l’Union. Le projet ELENA, financé par l’Union européenne, a depuis produit les premières plaquettes européennes.

Ces questions comptent particulièrement pour l’Europe. Une entreprise peut maîtriser la conception de sa technologie et rester dépendante d’équipements, de matériaux ou de procédés situés en amont de sa production. La nationalité du concepteur ne dit donc rien, à elle seule, de la souveraineté industrielle d’une technologie.

La course électorale dans le Michigan a été particulièrement médiatisée. Plusieurs États historiquement républicains, comme le Texas ou le Kansas, ont également élu des sénateurs démocrates, pour la première fois depuis des décennies.

Au-delà du signal symbolique que représente ce rejet de la politique de Trump, l’enjeu est aussi institutionnel : le Congrès demeure un contre-pouvoir fondamental à l’exécutif états-unien. Mais peut-on s’attendre à ce que cette vague bleue impacte réellement la politique extérieure états-unienne ?

title: Who Polices the Blockchain? The Binance Heist and the New Gatekeepers
text: Phantasmic theft: A fan of the television series Money Heist at an immersive installation in Turkey. Image: İdil Toffolo / Alamy StockThe institutions that have the authority to police international finance are no longer necessarily the institutions that possess the capabilities to do so.On 29 October, the largest heist in history took less than half an hour to unfold. The loss by Binance – the world’s largest crypto exchange – of US$6.3 billion became instant front-page news and led TV bulletins. Alongside the media headlines and breathless commentary and hot takes, the loss highlights three developments that are not new but are increasingly consequential for international financial security. First is scale. The digitalisation of finance has transformed the speed, reach and potential scale of financial crime. Just imagine how many banks would need to be raided to gather just a fraction of the loot secured from Binance. Second, borders. Criminals have long exploited the gaps between jurisdictions and the constraints placed on law enforcement by those boundaries. In a world dominated by digital financial services, as things stand, borders neuter governments’ abilities to respond. And third – most strikingly – control. Governments retain legal authority over financial activity, but the practical capability to identify, trace and interrupt illicit financial flows increasingly rests with privately held technology and financial sector companies.So, in this day and age, who actually polices the blockchain on which the crypto industry and those that attack it rely? And are governments and international institutions, including the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the global anti-financial crime watchdog, adapting sufficiently quickly to this very obvious redistribution of operational capability, or are they stuck in an analogue frame of mind?The Biggest Bank Robbery That Never HappenedAt the time of writing, it is still not entirely clear how Binance’s defences were so comprehensively breached. What is clear is that however long it took to plan and however technically complex the design of the operation, this heist was conducted remotely from across the globe, with no need to pull on a balaclava, threaten staff with a shotgun, and speed through the streets in a getaway car to safety. In essence, the crime was entirely risk-free; and with ever more financial and economic activity carried out and stored online, the size of the prize for those with the necessary patience and skill is immense. And when the ‘criminal’ is a state with motivation, purpose and years of experience to draw on, the result can be spectacular.quoteThe most important lesson of the past week is that while we may not be ‘post-government’, we are perhaps entering one in which governments cannot exercise meaningful financial control without the cooperation of companies whose international reach and technical capabilities exceed their own None of this is of course new. A fake $750 Apple Cash offer funnels users toward app and game promotions

Its device checks, countdown, and “spots left” claims aren’t real

Users get no reward and may share information or spend money in games

A page we found promises a $750 Apple Cash reward if you complete a quick “device verification.” There is no reward, and the page does not verify your device. Instead, it sends you to app offers through affiliate tracking links.

The page is not affiliated with Apple. If you’ve landed on a page like this, close it.

The fake page promises $750 in Apple Cash

Why Apple makes such good bait

Apple is one of the world’s most recognized brands, and scammers use that familiarity to make fake offers seem credible. Apple’s own scam guidance lists fake promotions offering free products and prizes among common tricks.

Current Apple news gives scammers useful cover. The new iPhone Duo is in the headlines, and we recently found a fake preorder page whose code tried to exploit older iPhones as soon as the page opened. With the iPhone Duo starting at $1,999, a promise of $750 in Apple money may catch people’s attention.

The word “verify” may also sound timely. Starting November 9, Green Dot Bank, which issues Apple Cash, will require some users to verify their identity before they can reload their balance. A fake page asking people to “verify your device” to get Apple Cash may seem more plausible in that context.

Apple Cash isn’t an Apple Gift Card

The page blurs two different things:

Apple Cash is money you send, receive and spend through Apple Wallet.

An Apple Gift Card adds money to your Apple Account balance for Apple purchases.

Apple warns that its gift cards can only be used for Apple purchases, and that someone asking you to pay them with one is probably a scammer. But neither Apple Cash nor an Apple Gift Card comes from a website that “unlocks” it after you install an app.

The fake site leans hard on Apple’s name. It calls the app it promotes an “Official Apple Partner” that is “Verified by Apple Cash,” and its footer claims “Copyright © 2026 Apple Inc.” None of that is true.

A “verification” that verifies nothing

We looked at the code behind the page’s three steps: Eligibility Check, Verify Device and Claim Reward.

The eligibility check is a timer. The four items that tick green, including “Location: United States,” are just labels that light up on a schedule. The page never checks where you are or what device you use. Everyone passes in under four seconds.

It tells users to download an app for “device verification”

The device verification is an app install. The page tell users to download an app called Reco Social, then tells them to create an account, and install and play a game. We found no evidence that Reco Social or its developer created or operated the fake reward page.

When you tap Download & Open App, the page opens a link in a new tab. Five seconds later, it starts showing “Verifying device…”. Nothing is being verified. The page has no way of knowing whether you installed anything, created an account or played a game.

The reward is the same link again. Ten minutes after you tap the button, the page moves on by itself and announces “Device Verified Successfully,” whether or not you installed anything. The Claim Your $750 button doesn’t add anything to your wallet. It opens the same link as the download button.

Fake urgency

The page is built to stop you from thinking too long:

“Only 47 spots left today” always starts at 47. It drops by one every 30 seconds and stops at 3, so it never runs out.

The “claimed $750” pop-ups are generated at random from a list of 15 first names and 15 US states, with a random “minutes ago.” Every visitor sees a new one every 8 to 15 seconds.

The 10-minute “Session Expires” countdown doesn’t end anything when it hits zero.

Who gets paid?

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an OpenAI Codex jailbreak bundle that's designed to modify an artificial intelligence (AI) agent's trusted instructions to insert advertisements for a third-party AI gateway.

The phenomenon has been codenamed prompt adware by Check Point Research.

Called Haiou (meaning Seagull in Chinese), the jailbreak modifies OpenAI Codex's configuration files to inject advertisements for the jailbreak author's website into subsequent agent responses.

"The advertised service is an opaque, OpenAI-compatible LLM gateway, a middleware between an application and an LLM provider," Check Point Research said in a technical report. "The likely business model is to use the freely distributed jailbreak bundle as an acquisition channel for the paid gateway service."

Adware is a type of software that displays unwanted advertisements, which can appear on users' computers or mobile devices, often in the form of pop-ups or banners. Prompt adware extends this sketchy behavior to AI agents by means of a jailbreak that defeats the model's safety training and content guardrails.

The idea is to persistently modify the agent's global instructions through natural language to influence future responses. This, in turn, causes common greetings or activation words like "Seagull," "hi," "hello," "hey," "yo," and "are you there?" to trigger an advertisement for "zz.aiapi2025[.]top."

Haiou attempts to jailbreak a model by using several prompt injection techniques, such as role-playing and reframing cybersecurity-related requests into a Capture The Flag (CTF) scenario. In addition, it installs security-focused skills devoted to penetration testing, cracking, and reverse engineering.

However, it doesn't stop there. The bundle also injects persistent ads into the global agent instruction file to promote the LLM gateway website. On GitHub, "haiou-codex" is advertised as a "local enhancement configuration package" that adds a "Chinese technical personality and security research workflow to Codex." As of writing, the repository has been forked 77 times and starred 403 times since it was made available on July 10, 2026.

It's worth noting that Codex is not officially available in mainland China, suggesting that the service is likely aimed at individuals or organizations wanting to try out Western AI coding assistants.

What's more, the jailbreak has been bundled within Codex-X, an open-source Chinese visualization tool for configuring Codex through a graphical user interface.

"The behavior is introduced through natural-language instructions and configuration, rather than a traditional executable payload that users and security teams may more readily recognize as software behavior," Pedro Drimel Neto, malware analysis team leader at Check Point, said.

While serving an ad may seem relatively harmless in the larger scheme of things, the findings demonstrate how a bad actor could introduce undesirable behavior through third-party skills or configurations, leading to supply chain attacks.

"As AI agents become part of enterprise environments, the prompts, Skills and third-party components influencing their behavior become part of the trust chain too," Neto said.

Two Canadian men face federal prosecution in New York after allegedly orchestrating a multi-year cyber incursion campaign that hijacked computing resources across American universities to secretly mine cryptocurrency.

A federal grand jury indicted Ryan James Roach, 35, of Saskatchewan, and Mathiew James Stubbings, 41, of Ontario, on charges of conspiracy to obtain information and cause damage to protected computers, obtaining information from a protected computer, and intentional computer damage.

Roach was extradited from Canada on October 28, while extradition proceedings against Stubbings remain underway before Canadian courts.

According to the indictment, the intrusions spanned from June 2016 through December 2019, compromising systems at academic institutions in New York, Massachusetts, North Carolina, and Tennessee.

The two allegedly set up multi-country virtual private server infrastructure using fraudulent identities to manage the campaign. “These servers transmitted malware and mining software to victim computers and stored stolen login credentials,” the DOJ explained.

The threat actors specifically singled out campuses maintaining supercomputers, using previously compromised machines as pivot points to conceal their origins.

Canadian court filings revealed that the hijacked university hardware was repurposed to mine a cryptocurrency called Electroneum.

“Once inside a network, Roach and Stubbings used sophisticated techniques and tools to conduct reconnaissance and expand their access within the network,” prosecutors stated.

If convicted, the offenses carry a maximum statutory penalty of 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine on each count.
